newsitem.title: UK: Major to rally UK Conservatives with health pledge.
newsitem.headline: Major to rally UK Conservatives with health pledge.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major on Friday unveils the first commitment of an "opportunity for all" manifesto that he hopes will win a fifth consecutive term of office for his Conservatives at the coming election.

Buoyed by the party's new-found eagerness to put differences over Europe on ice, Major will wrap up its annual conference with a promise to continue to increase spending in real terms on the state-run National Health Service (NHS) if reelected.

Aides said the speech aimed to build on the relaxed performance by the prime minister at an unscripted question-and- answer session on Wednesday that drew glowing reviews, confirming Major as a prime asset in the campaign for the general election now no more than seven months away.
Although denigrated in the press as the grey man of British politics, Major is more popular than the party he heads, which voters see as tired after 17-1/2 years in power.

Conservative sources said Major wanted to make health the centrepiece of a "personal statement" to the conference because he attached huge importance to the NHS. He also believed the opposition Labour party's health policies were confused.
The Conservatives have increased spending on the NHS, over and above inflation, by 12 percent since Major won the last election in 1992. Its budget is now about 42 billion pounds ($65 billion).
A senior aide said the pledge to keep spending more would be coupled with plans to give doctors and hospitals more power to run their own affairs.
Together they make up Major's "health service guarantee".
Major has spoken emotionally at past conferences of the care his late parents received in the hands of the NHS and how its doctors helped him recover from a serious car crash.
The new commitments will catapult health to the forefront of the looming election battle.
Labour, which heads the Conservatives in opinion polls by 20 percentage points, has pledged to cut NHS waiting lists by 100,000 if it recaptures power for the first time since 1979.
The health plans follow commitments unveiled by ministers earlier in the week to strengthen Britain's economy, reform the welfare state, crack down on crime and boost education.

Major will bracket them as "the five opportunities" and argue that only the Conservatives can deliver them -- despite broadly similar pledges that Labour leader Tony Blair has put at the heart of his pre-election blueprint.

A senior Conservative source said Blair might claim to be a reformer, but Labour's record since 1979 showed that it had bitterly resisted the sweeping social and economic reforms that Major wanted to build on in a fifth Consecutive term.
How to enable ordinary people to seize opportunities will be the "great divide" between the parties at the coming election, Major will say.

Aides said they did not expect Major to appeal himself for unity in the party, which has been deeply divided over Britain's role in Europe, because other ministers had already successfully done the job for him.

Finance minister Kenneth Clarke and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine won long standing ovations on Thursday for powerful speeches that rallied the party faithful and banished -- at least for now -- all talk of damaging splits over Europe.
